teaser: The most powerful official in Burgundy had himself painted as the Virgin's equal.
review_notes:
Rogier van der Weyden's Saint Luke Drawing the Virgin (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, c. 1435-40) is generally agreed to derive from this composition.
Panel size about 66 x 62 cm. Painted for Rolin's chapel in Notre-Dame-du-Chatel, Autun; church destroyed in the 1790s; in the Louvre since 1800.
Rolin born in Autun around 1376, chancellor of Philip the Good from 1422.
Large purse at Rolin's belt in the underdrawing, left out of the final paint: reported by Louvre technical studies.
Man in the red headdress as a possible Van Eyck self-reference: a suggestion, not established.
Tiny cross on the bridge and its link to the 1419 murder of John the Fearless at Montereau: not used in the lesson.
Chronicler's remark on Rolin (Jacques du Clercq) is paraphrased, not quoted.
Hospices de Beaune founded in 1443 by Rolin and his wife Guigone de Salins; annual charity wine auction still held each November.
Louvre restoration 2021-2024 and the 2024 exhibition devoted to the painting.
Carved capitals above Rolin (Expulsion from Eden, Cain and Abel, Noah's drunkenness) are not legible in the working image and are not pointed at.

lesson.text: In Boston hangs a painting by Rogier van der Weyden. Saint Luke kneels on the left, the Virgin sits on the right, and between them three openings give onto a garden where two small people lean on a wall and watch a river. Rogier did not invent that arrangement. He had seen it, a few years earlier, in this panel by Jan van Eyck.

The original is small, about 66 by 62 centimeters (26 by 24 inches). On the left, in a gown of brown and gold brocade trimmed with fur, kneels the man who ordered it: Nicolas Rolin. Facing him are Mary and the infant Christ, with an angel about to set a crown on her head.

Rolin was born into an ordinary family in the town of Autun around 1376. He became a lawyer, and in 1422 Duke Philip the Good made him chancellor of Burgundy, the head of the government. He held the post for some forty years and grew enormously rich. He wanted this picture for his family chapel in the church where he was baptized.

Buyers often appeared in religious paintings, and there were rules. You were shown smaller than the holy figures, or off to one side, with a patron saint standing behind you to make the introduction. Now see what Rolin asked for.
Four lines show how the scene is balanced, and how bold that balance is.

lines.label: Same height
lines.text: Rolin's head and Mary's sit on one level. He is exactly her size, in the same room, on the same floor. No saint stands between them.

lines.label: His gaze
lines.text: He does not bow his head. His eyes go straight across, toward the child, though they seem to stop a little short. He may be seeing all this in his mind as he prays.

lines.label: The blessing
lines.text: The child raises two fingers toward Rolin's joined hands. In his other hand he holds a crystal globe topped with a jeweled cross: the world, in the palm of a baby.

lines.label: The middle
lines.text: The floor tiles, the gap between the columns and the river all run up the center. Nothing occupies the middle of the picture except distance.

lesson.text: So the two halves are weighed like a pair of scales: a mortal on one side, heaven on the other, at equal height. The open prayer book on Rolin's desk supports the idea of a vision. He has been reading, he looks up, and what he was praying to is there.

Rolin first looked even richer. Imaging of the layers under the paint shows that Van Eyck drew a large purse hanging from the chancellor's belt, then left it out. Someone decided that a money bag in front of the Virgin was one detail too many.

And the center, where nothing happens? Van Eyck put a world in it. Through the three arches you step onto a terrace, cross a garden, and then the ground drops away to a river valley that runs to snow-covered mountains. On the real panel this view is about the size of a hand.

lesson.title: Through the arches
lesson.text: Go outward, from the terrace to the horizon.

spots.title: Two onlookers
spots.text: Two men stand at the battlements with their backs to us. One peers down through a gap in the wall. The other wears a red headdress like the one Van Eyck wears in a likely self-portrait.

spots.title: The bridge
spots.text: A stone bridge on a row of arches links the two banks, with a tower at one end. On the original you can make out people crossing it, each one a single touch of the brush.

spots.title: Blue distance
spots.text: An island with a castle, then hills fading to pale blue and white peaks. Far things look bluer and hazier in real life. Painting them that way is called aerial perspective.

spots.title: The right bank
spots.text: Behind the Virgin the city bristles with church towers and spires. The bank behind Rolin is plainer: houses, one church, hills covered in green.

lesson.text: That difference between the banks is probably deliberate. His side looks like the everyday world, with slopes that resemble the vineyards he owned. Her side looks like a city of churches. The river runs between, and the bridge suggests that there is a way across.
In 1443 Rolin and his wife founded a hospital for the poor in the town of Beaune, paid for by vineyards. It still exists, and so does the funding: a charity wine auction is held there every November.

Was that generosity or insurance for his soul? People at the time already wondered. One chronicler wrote, in effect, that Rolin was very wise in worldly matters and that he would rather not comment on the spiritual ones. Van Eyck may have slipped his own opinion into the garden.
A bird known for showing off is strolling on the terrace. Where is it?

spots.title: Peacocks
spots.text: Two peacocks, one perched on the wall and one walking below with its long tail trailing. They sit right beside Rolin's praying hands.

lesson.text: A peacock could mean two things then. Its flesh was believed never to rot, so it stood for eternal life. It was also, as it is now, the bird of pride. Placed at the chancellor's fingertips, it lets you choose your reading, which may have been the safest way to paint a man this powerful.

From 2021 to 2024 the Louvre cleaned the panel, the first major treatment since it entered the museum in 1800. Layers of yellowed varnish came off, and the landscape, which had turned greenish and flat, got back its cold blues and its depth.

Go back to Rogier's Saint Luke. What he took from Van Eyck was more than a pose: it was the discovery that a small opening at the back of a room can hold the whole world, and change the meaning of everyone standing in front of it.

quiz.question: Who was Nicolas Rolin?
options: The chancellor of Burgundy, head of the duke's government
quiz.explanation: Duke Philip the Good made him chancellor in 1422.

quiz.question: What was unusual about how Rolin is shown?
options: He is the same size as the Virgin, with no saint presenting him
He stands with his back to the Virgin
He is shown as a child
quiz.explanation: Donors were normally smaller or introduced by a saint; Rolin kneels as Mary's equal.

quiz.question: What did Van Eyck draw at Rolin's belt and then leave out?
quiz.explanation: The drawing under the paint shows a big purse that never made it into the final picture.

quiz.question: What is aerial perspective?
options: Showing a scene from a bird's point of view
Making distant things paler and bluer
quiz.explanation: Far hills are painted hazier and bluer, as they look in real life.

quiz.question: Which two meanings could a peacock carry?
quiz.explanation: Its flesh was believed not to rot, and it was also the bird of pride.

facts.text: A patron saint stands behind Rolin to introduce him to the Virgin.
facts.explanation: No saint is present; Rolin faces Mary and the child on his own.

facts.text: Rolin founded a hospital in Beaune that is still funded by a wine auction.
facts.explanation: He and his wife founded it in 1443 and paid for it with vineyards.

facts.text: The landscape seen through the arches fills a canvas several meters wide.
facts.explanation: The whole panel is about 66 by 62 centimeters, and the view is roughly the size of a hand.
